articles.title: हरियाणा में कमजोर पड़ा मानसून, पश्चिमी हवाओं ने बढ़ाया तापमान, दिन में चढ़ेगा पारा - ETV Bharat
articles.search_term: ("पारा चढ़ा" OR "पारा पहुंचा" OR तापमान OR "तापमान बढ़ा" OR "रिकॉर्ड तोड़ गर्मी" OR "डिग्री सेल्सियस" OR "पारा उबला" OR "अधिकतम तापमान" OR "तापमान 40 पार" OR "तापमान 45 पार" OR "तापमान बढ़ने की संभावना") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
चंडीगढ़:हरियाणा में मानसून की रफ्तार अब धीमी पड़ गई है और कई इलाकों में बारिश का दौर थम गया है. मौसम विभाग के अनुसार 8 सितंबर से प्रदेश में मानसून की सक्रियता कम होने की संभावना है. आने वाले दिनों में बारिश की बजाय गर्मी का असर बढ़ सकता है.
12 सितंबर तक बदलता रहेगा मौसम:मौसम वैज्ञानिकों की मानें तो 12 सितंबर तक हरियाणा में मौसम आमतौर पर परिवर्तनशील बना रहेगा. इस दौरान कहीं-कहीं आंशिक बादल छाए रह सकते हैं, लेकिन व्यापक बारिश की संभावना कम है. पश्चिमी हवाओं के प्रभाव से दिन के तापमान में बढ़ोतरी दर्ज की जा सकती है. पिछले 24 घंटों में प्रदेश के औसत अधिकतम तापमान में 2.7 डिग्री सेल्सियस की बढ़ोतरी हुई है. पश्चिमी हवाओं के चलते गर्मी का असर बढ़ने लगा है और कई जिलों में तापमान सामान्य से ऊपर पहुंच गया है.
हिसार सबसे गर्म:प्रदेश में हिसार सबसे गर्म जिला रहा, जहां अधिकतम तापमान 38.3 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया. यह सामान्य से 2.6 डिग्री अधिक है. वहीं भिवानी में 36.5 डिग्री, चरखी दादरी में 36.3 डिग्री, सिरसा में 35.9 डिग्री और फरीदाबाद व पलवल में 35.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस तापमान रिकॉर्ड किया गया.
न्यूनतम तापमान में मामूली गिरावट: प्रदेश के औसत न्यूनतम तापमान में हालांकि 0.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस की मामूली गिरावट दर्ज की गई. सबसे कम न्यूनतम तापमान रेवाड़ी के बावल में 22.8 डिग्री सेल्सियस रिकॉर्ड हुआ. दिन में गर्मी बढ़ने के बावजूद सुबह और रात के तापमान में फिलहाल ज्यादा बदलाव देखने को नहीं मिला है.
कम दबाव के क्षेत्र से कमजोर हुई मानसूनी गतिविधियां:मौसम विभाग के अनुसार मानसूनी टर्फ रेखा की स्थिति और उत्तर प्रदेश के ऊपर बने कम दबाव के क्षेत्र का असर हरियाणा के मौसम पर पड़ रहा है. इसके कारण प्रदेश में मानसून की गतिविधियां कमजोर हो गई हैं और व्यापक बारिश की संभावना कम हो गई है. मौसम वैज्ञानिक डॉ. मदन खीचड़ ने कहा कि, "8 सितंबर से हरियाणा में मानसून की सक्रियता कम होने की संभावना है. 12 सितंबर तक मौसम परिवर्तनशील रहेगा और बीच-बीच में आंशिक बादल छा सकते हैं. पश्चिमी हवाएं चलने से तापमान में बढ़ोतरी होगी. प्रदेश में कहीं-कहीं गरज-चमक के साथ छिटपुट बारिश हो सकती है, लेकिन फिलहाल व्यापक बारिश की संभावना नहीं है. ऐसे में अगले कुछ दिनों तक हरियाणा के लोगों को दिन में बढ़ती गर्मी का सामना करना पड़ सकता है, जबकि मानसून की सक्रियता कमजोर बनी रहने के आसार हैं."

articles.title: 8 सितंबर, 2026 के लिए मौसम पूर्वानुमान: ठंडी हवा का एक बड़ा हिस्सा उत्तर की ओर बढ़ने वाला है, जिससे गरज के साथ बारिश होगी। - Vietnam.vn

articles.full_text:
8 सितंबर, 2026 के लिए मौसम पूर्वानुमान: ठंडी हवा का एक बड़ा हिस्सा उत्तर की ओर बढ़ने वाला है, जिससे गरज के साथ बारिश होगी।
8 सितंबर, 2026 के लिए मौसम पूर्वानुमान: उत्तरी वियतनाम में मौसम के पहले शीत मोर्चे के आने से पहले कुछ गर्म मौसम रहेगा, जिसके साथ गरज के साथ बारिश होगी। मध्य वियतनाम से लेकर मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी वियतनाम तक, दोपहर और शाम के बाद कुछ स्थानों पर भारी बारिश होने की संभावना है।
VietNamNet•07/09/2026
राष्ट्रीय जल-मौसम विज्ञान पूर्वानुमान केंद्र के अनुसार, उत्तरी क्षेत्र में सामान्य शरद ऋतु का मौसम है, जिसमें कम बारिश और भरपूर धूप है। हालांकि, इस क्षेत्र का मौसम जल्द ही बदलेगा क्योंकि समय से पहले आने वाला उत्तर-पूर्वी मानसून आ रहा है, जिससे मध्य क्षेत्र में भी बारिश बढ़ जाएगी।
विशेष रूप से, 8 सितंबर को उत्तरी क्षेत्र में धूप वाला मौसम बना रहेगा और अधिकतम तापमान लगभग 35 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा; दोपहर बाद और शाम को कुछ क्षेत्रों में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है।
9 से 11 सितंबर के बीच, उत्तरी वियतनाम में इस मौसम के पहले शीत मोर्चे का प्रभाव पड़ने की संभावना है।
कमजोर शीत मोर्चे के प्रभाव के कारण, 9 से 11 सितंबर तक, टोंकिन की खाड़ी के उत्तरी भाग में 5 की तीव्रता वाली, कभी-कभी 6 की तीव्रता वाली, तेज उत्तरपूर्वी हवाएँ चलेंगी, जिनमें 2-3 मीटर ऊंची लहरें होंगी; समुद्र अशांत रहेगा।
लगभग 9-10 सितंबर के आसपास उत्तरी क्षेत्र में बारिश, बौछारें और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है। दिन का अधिकतम तापमान 33 डिग्री सेल्सियस से नीचे और रात का न्यूनतम तापमान 25 डिग्री सेल्सियस से नीचे गिर जाएगा। मध्य और पहाड़ी क्षेत्रों में तापमान 22 डिग्री सेल्सियस से नीचे जा सकता है, जिससे रातें और सुबह ठंडी रहेंगी।
विशेष रूप से 8 सितंबर को हनोई में मौसम धूप वाला रहेगा, कुछ क्षेत्रों में गर्मी रहेगी और अधिकतम तापमान 35 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच सकता है; रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है। 9 से 11 सितंबर तक शहर में बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आ सकता है, तापमान में गिरावट आएगी और मौसम सुहावना हो जाएगा।
इस बीच, 8 सितंबर की दोपहर और रात को, क्वांग त्रि से दा नांग शहर तक का क्षेत्र, क्वांग न्गाई प्रांत का पूर्वी भाग, मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी क्षेत्र में बारिश और छिटपुट गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है।
गौरतलब है कि उत्तर-पूर्वी मानसून के प्रभाव और उष्णकटिबंधीय अभिसरण क्षेत्र की सक्रियता के कारण, 10 सितंबर से मध्य क्षेत्र में व्यापक स्तर पर लंबे समय तक भारी बारिश होने की संभावना है।
मौसम विज्ञान एजेंसी ने चेतावनी दी है कि आंधी-तूफान के दौरान लोगों को बवंडर, बिजली गिरने, ओले गिरने और तेज हवाओं से सावधान रहना चाहिए। स्थानीय स्तर पर भारी बारिश से छोटी नदियों और नालों में अचानक बाढ़ आ सकती है, ढलानों पर भूस्खलन हो सकता है और निचले इलाकों में जलभराव हो सकता है।
देश के सभी क्षेत्रों के लिए 8 सितंबर, 2026 का मौसम पूर्वानुमान:
हनोई
दिन में बादल छाए रहेंगे, धूप निकलेगी, शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश होगी। हल्की हवा चलेगी।
दिन में बीच-बीच में धूप के साथ बादल छाए रहेंगे, शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है। हवा हल्की चलेगी।
न्यूनतम तापमान: 22-25 डिग्री सेल्सियस, कुछ स्थानों पर 22 डिग्री सेल्सियस से नीचे। अधिकतम तापमान: 31-34 डिग्री सेल्सियस, कुछ स्थानों पर 34 डिग्री सेल्सियस से ऊपर।
पूर्वोत्तर वियतनाम
दिन में बीच-बीच में धूप के साथ बादल छाए रहेंगे, शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है। हवा हल्की चलेगी।
न्यूनतम तापमान: 24-27 डिग्री सेल्सियस, पर्वतीय क्षेत्रों में 23 डिग्री सेल्सियस से नीचे। अधिकतम तापमान: 32-35 डिग्री सेल्सियस।
आसमान में बादल छाए रहेंगे और कुछ इलाकों में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है; दक्षिण में दोपहर और शाम के दौरान छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की आशंका है, साथ ही कुछ स्थानों पर भारी बारिश भी हो सकती है। हवा हल्की रहेगी। गरज के साथ तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की संभावना है।
आसमान में बादल छाए रहेंगे और कुछ इलाकों में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है; विशेषकर उत्तर में, दोपहर और शाम के दौरान बारिश और छिटपुट गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है, साथ ही कुछ स्थानों पर भारी बारिश भी हो सकती है। दक्षिण-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 तीव्रता की हवाएं चलेंगी। गरज के साथ तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की संभावना है।
न्यूनतम तापमान: 25-28 डिग्री। अधिकतम तापमान: 32-35 डिग्री, कुछ क्षेत्रों में 35 डिग्री से अधिक भी हो सकता है।
मध्य उच्चभूमि
आसमान में बादल छाए रहेंगे और कुछ इलाकों में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी, खासकर दोपहर और शाम के समय। छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ सकती हैं, और कुछ जगहों पर भारी बारिश भी हो सकती है। दक्षिण-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 तीव्रता की हवाएं चलेंगी। गरज के साथ बौछारों के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने, ओले पड़ने और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की संभावना है।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
न्यूनतम तापमान: 20-23 डिग्री। अधिकतम तापमान: 26-29 डिग्री, कुछ क्षेत्रों में 29 डिग्री से अधिक भी हो सकता है।
दक्षिणी वियतनाम
आसमान में बादल छाए रहेंगे, कुछ इलाकों में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है, खासकर दोपहर और शाम के बाद। कुछ स्थानों पर भारी बारिश भी हो सकती है। दक्षिण-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 तीव्रता की हवाएं चलेंगी। तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने, ओले पड़ने और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की संभावना है।

हो ची मिन्ह सिटी
दिन में बादल छाए रहेंगे, धूप निकलेगी; दोपहर और शाम को छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी, कुछ इलाकों में भारी बारिश हो सकती है; रात में भी छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी। दक्षिण-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 की गति से हवाएं चलेंगी। गरज के साथ बौछारों के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली, ओले और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की संभावना है।

As extreme heat waves intensify due to recent climate change, railway rail temperatures now exceed 60°C during summer, increasing track deformation risks. This has necessitated speed restrictions, causing delays and raising safety concerns as a social issue.
The Korea Railroad Research Institute (KRRI) (President: Sagong Myung) has developed the world's first "rail-mounted thermal-blocking textile with automated installation and retrieval system" to dramatically mitigate temperature rises on railway tracks during extreme summer heat.
Currently, rail temperature reduction during summer relies almost entirely on water-spraying systems, which have significant limitations: high installation costs and continuous water consumption. Therefore, a water-free, cost-effective alternative has been strongly needed.
KRRI's technology lowers rail temperatures by attaching a special heat-blocking textile to the rail using magnetic force to block solar radiation. The "heat-blocking textile" features a multilayer structure composed of a special coating that reflects more than 85% of solar radiation, combined with magnets and fiberglass layers. Once installed, the system requires no additional operating costs and poses no risk of failure, offering both stability and economic efficiency.
Field demonstrations were completed on the Gwangju Line of the conventional railway network in the summer of 2024 and on the Jungbu Inland High-Speed Line in the summer of 2025. The results verified a maximum rail temperature reduction of 10.9°C, with no performance degradation observed after testing. The technology was stably applied to both conventional and high-speed rail types*, and certified testing confirmed outstanding durability, with performance maintained for more than 10 years.
KRRI also developed a fully integrated "all-in-one automated system" that covers the complete lifecycle from installation through retrieval of the thermal-blocking textile. The system enables all operations from cleaning foreign substances off rail surfaces, applying the textile, to retrieving it after the summer season with a single piece of equipment. Its modular design allows two operators to easily transport, assemble, and disassemble it, and the system can operate at speeds exceeding 2 km per hour, significantly reducing both time and cost.
KRRI verified the safety and durability of the thermal-blocking textile technology. The system remained secure even under strong opposing winds generated by KTX trains traveling at 300 km/h. The magnetic attachment force was optimized to withstand wind speeds of up to 66 m/s (1.5 times stronger than high-speed train-induced wind), and additional dual fastening mechanisms were applied to ensure that the textile remains firmly attached even during high-speed train operation.
The technology's excellence was further recognized at the "2025 Seoul International Invention Exhibition (December 3 to 6, 2025, COEX Hall C, Seoul)," hosted by the Korean Intellectual Property Office and the Korea Invention Promotion Association. The thermal-blocking textile patent won the Grand Prize, and the automated equipment patent received the Silver Prize. Additionally, at the "2025 New Technology Commercialization Promotion Conference (December 10, 2025, Peace & Park Convention, Seoul)" hosted by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and the Korea Industrial Technology Association, the technology obtained National New Excellent Technology (NET, Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy Certification No. 1594), further validating its innovation.
KRRI has finalized a technology transfer agreement with PITCHCABLE Co., Ltd. (CEO: Lim Dong-wook) for the heat-blocking textile and its installation·retrieval technology, ensuring full linkage to commercialization and completing the research-to-application cycle.
This technology was developed as part of KRRI's in-house research program under the National Research Council of Science & Technology (NST) (Chairman: Kim Young-sik).
Chief Researcher Kang Dong-hoon at KRRI stated, "This technology goes beyond simply lowering rail temperatures - it presents a new paradigm for protecting railway safety in the era of climate crisis. We plan to expand its application beyond railways to various fields that require heat mitigation, such as building exteriors and roadside facilities."
President Sagong Myung of KRRI said, "This is a demand-driven research outcome that allows the public to use railways with confidence even during extreme summer heat. In an era where climate crisis directly translates into national risk, we will further advance this technology to ensure safe railway operations and expand its application to overseas markets."

Kerala faces power shortage as intense heat drives up electricity demand
Restrictions may continue after consumption rises by up to 800 MW, while temperatures remain 3–4 degrees Celsius above normal
Kerala is grappling with unusually high temperatures and mounting pressure on its electricity supply, with power restrictions likely to continue in several areas as demand rises sharply.
The state recorded a maximum temperature of 36.2 degrees Celsius on Monday. The India Meteorological Department has forecast that temperatures will remain 3–4 degrees above normal on Tuesday.
The persistent heat has led households and commercial establishments to increase their use of cooling appliances. According to the Kerala State Electricity Board, the resulting surge in consumption has pushed demand up by as much as 800 MW.
The board-imposed restrictions lasting up to an hour in several areas on Monday after it was unable to secure sufficient electricity from outside Kerala during peak hours. Similar measures could remain in place if consumption continues at the same level on Tuesday.
The KSEB attributed the supply constraints to the absence of short-term power agreements and high prices in the real-time electricity market, which have made emergency purchases difficult.
Although tenders were invited to secure additional electricity for September, the board reportedly received no offers from suppliers willing to provide power during peak-demand hours. This has left it with limited capacity to address the unexpected increase in consumption.
Amid the severe weather, the Kerala State Disaster Management Authority has issued precautionary guidelines to reduce the risk of sunstroke, heat exhaustion and dehydration.
Residents have been advised to avoid direct exposure to sunlight during the hottest hours, consume sufficient water and watch for symptoms linked to heat-related illnesses.
The heat warning will remain in effect until 9 September, with temperatures expected to stay considerably above seasonal levels across Kerala. Continued hot weather and elevated electricity consumption could place further strain on the state’s power supply until temperatures begin to ease.

France's wine vats are on track to be the emptiest they've been in roughly seven decades. The nation's Agriculture Ministry says 2026 output is expected to slip another 6% from 2025's already record-low level, to about 900 million gallons—about 17% below the 2021–2025 average, per France 24. That would make it the lowest output since 1957, according to the International Organisation of Vine and Wine. Blame a one-two punch of shrinking vineyards and brutal summer heat and drought, which slammed yields unevenly across regions.
"Conditions had initially looked promising, with good grape development and low disease pressure," notes Politico. "But 'the hot and dry conditions of the summer degraded this potential,'" according to the Agricultural Ministry's stats service. Champagne is set to be hit hardest, with production forecast to be about half of both last year's level and the five-year average, per France 24. Languedoc-Roussillon is a rare bright spot, with a modest rebound from 2025, though still below its recent five-year average. Paris has pledged more than $1.2 billion in emergency aid for farmers, a sum that industry groups argue doesn't cover the damage.

ENVIRONMENT NEWS - A very strong El Niño event is developing in the Pacific Ocean and could intensify further this spring, raising concerns about below-normal rainfall, soaring temperatures and potentially severe heatwaves across southern Africa.
The latest weekly average sea surface temperature anomalies in the eastern-central tropical Pacific have already exceeded the threshold used to define a very strong El Niño, according to the South African Weather Service (SAWS).
Current forecasts indicate that the event could exceed the 3°C threshold, potentially making the 2026/27 El Niño the strongest event in living memory.
Drier and warmer conditions expected
El Niño events are statistically associated with below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures across much of southern Africa.
Some of the region’s most impactful El Niño events - including those of 1982/83 and 2015/16 - were associated with widespread drought.
However, the relationship is not absolute. The very strong 1997/98 El Niño, for example, was associated with slightly above-normal rainfall in parts of South Africa’s summer rainfall region.
This means that while below-normal rainfall is currently the most likely outcome for southern Africa this summer, an El Niño event does not automatically result in drought.
The latest SAWS seasonal forecast for October to December nevertheless points to below-normal rainfall over most of South Africa, while above-normal temperatures are also expected.
A similar outlook applies to the November to January 2027 period, with drier and warmer conditions the most likely outcome across much of the country.
Heatwaves could become more frequent
The combination of a very strong El Niño and ongoing global warming could make the coming summer particularly challenging.
SAWS says 2027 is likely to be the warmest year ever recorded if the expected strength of the 2026/27 El Niño materialises alongside continued global warming.
The previous very strong El Niño, in 2015/16, was associated with unprecedented heatwaves in southern Africa. Since then, the region has continued to warm, potentially increasing the impact of another major El Niño event.
If the forecast below-normal rainfall occurs, it could create conditions in which heatwaves become more frequent and potentially more severe.
The combination of prolonged dry conditions and extreme heat could also place additional pressure on water resources and weather-sensitive sectors.
Forecasts will be closely monitored
Despite the concerning outlook, SAWS cautions that uncertainty remains over the eventual strength of the El Niño and how it will affect different parts of southern Africa.
The extent of heatwaves and possible water scarcity will therefore be closely monitored, with information shared with Disaster Management structures, weather-sensitive industries, the media and the public.
SAWS is urging the public and weather-sensitive industries to keep up to date with its monthly seasonal forecasts as well as daily short-term weather forecasts.
These updates will be particularly important as the summer progresses and provide the latest guidance on heatwaves and other potentially high-impact weather events.
What is El Niño?
El Niño refers to an abnormal warming of the eastern-central tropical Pacific Ocean.
A strong El Niño is defined by three-month average sea surface temperatures in this region being more than 1.5°C above the long-term average. During a very strong El Niño, temperatures are more than 2°C above normal.
Current forecasts suggest the 2026/27 event could exceed 3°C - a level that would place it among the most extreme El Niño events on record.
For South Africans, the key message is to prepare rather than panic: rainfall and temperature forecasts will continue to be updated as the event develops, and conditions can vary significantly from one region to another.

articles.title: Post-heatwave nutrition advice for autumn crop success - Farmers Weekly
articles.search_term: (heatwave OR "heat wave" OR "severe heatwave" OR "extreme heat" OR "heat spell" OR "scorching heat" OR "blistering heat" OR "sweltering heat" OR "hot winds" OR loo OR "hot loo winds" OR "intense heat" OR "unbearable heat" OR "deadly heat" OR heat OR "weather forecast" OR "weather update" OR "weather alert" OR "IMD forecast" OR "IMD prediction" OR "IMD alert" OR IMD OR "rising temperatures" OR "temperatures expected to rise" OR "relief from heat" OR "respite from heat" OR "heat respite" OR "respite from scorching heat") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
Informed nutrition decisions this autumn will be critical to establishing crops and strengthening resilience across arable systems, following the summer heatwave.
Maximising every kilogram of nitrogen applied will require strong crop emergence and a well-rounded nutrition programme.
See also: Later-drilled oilseed rape requires tailored agronomy
“Setting crops up properly to receive that first application of spring nitrogen as efficiently as possible is so important,” says Agrii national fertiliser manager Tom Land.
“Much of this comes down to creating optimum root structure and mass to ensure full use of every kg of N,” he stresses.
Larger, early N dose advised
With growers likely in for a wet autumn and winter following the prolonged dry summer, conditions could soon get challenging.
Tom is advising larger doses of up to 80kg/ha N in the first fertiliser application window to build biomass both above and below ground.
“We are seeing milder autumns followed by a wet January and February, with late frosts followed by a dry period.
“This results in a shorter timeframe for cereal crops to take up and utilise N fertiliser,” he says.
Cereals require about 160kg/ha N to build a canopy sufficient of delivering a basic yield. However, growers should always consider residual N.
“Late applications of fertiliser to dry soils will reduce N uptake as fertiliser cannot be moved into the rooting zone.
“Some fertilisers will be lost to volatilisation. Obviously, it’s important to avoid waterlogged soils as well,” says Tom.
He recommends 80kg/ha N for winter wheat in the first dose. “Winter barley responds to early N protecting tiller numbers so consider splitting your total N requirement in half and applying 50% pre GS30 and the balance pre GS32.”
Crops like oilseed rape can move quickly into the spring and you only get time for a couple of applications.
A key benefit of this year’s early harvest is growers now have ample time to focus on setting up seed-beds and building the foundation for solid crop performance.
Tom discusses four key areas that growers can focus on this autumn to help achieve optimum production at harvest 2027 and build greater resilience longer term.
1. Focus on a soil pH of 7
Maintaining soil pH at the correct level of pH 7 is key to supporting optimum nutrient availability, long-term soil health and importantly, financial resilience.
“It’s definitely an area that it is too frequently overlooked, but it’s essential to get this right. Autumn is the best time to take action,” says Tom.
The earlier harvest is giving grower’s a great opportunity to get soil pH tested and get lime on the land where it is needed.
An overly acidic soil can see between 16% and 51% of applied fertiliser not taken up by the plant, with significantly reduced nitrogen use efficiency (NUE).
“At current prices, this translates to a cost of £63-£220/ha of unutilised fertiliser based on 190kg N/ha, 55kg P/ha, 85kg K/ha.”
As well as benefiting from improved NUE and yields, there are other advantages to be gained from maintaining the correct soil pH.
“For a start, it prevents acid-favouring weeds taking hold, but it also helps with disease prevention, inhibits transposition and movement of heavy metals that can lock up key nutrients and increases soil microbial activity.
“It’s important to give liming and soil pH the same level of attention and accuracy as the rest of the nutrient planning process.”
2. Make full use of phosphate
Adequate phosphate (P) uptake is essential to crop establishment and all-important root mass. The autumn period is the perfect time to address this.
While UK soils contain substantial reserves of phosphorus, only a small proportion is readily available to crops.
This makes managing soil conditions and P availability important when establishing crops following a challenging summer.
“It’s not just about making the correct applications. Getting soil phosphate mobilised and absorbed by crops is important,” says Tom.
Soils over chalk or limestone have high levels of calcium, which increases soil pH and locks up phosphate.
A soil phosphorus activator can help unlock P and improve nutrient availability. Agrii’s soil applied Agrii-Start Release works on calcium, aluminium and iron cations to displace locked-up phosphate.
According to Agrii R&D, the approach can release 40kg/ha of locked-up phosphate from the soil, reducing fertiliser expenditure and increasing winter wheat yields by as much as 1t/ha.
“In two years of trials with wheat set at a price of £180/t, the improvements in margin range from around £60/ha to more than £120/ha giving a return on investment of £36/ha to £81/ha.
“Don’t forget the saving made on applied fertilisers and the environmental gains by ensuring P is taken up by crops.”
3. Protect against stress using zinc, potassium and magnesium
Nutrients such as zinc, potassium and magnesium play an important role protecting crops against the effects of stress, particularly drought and heat.
- Potassium (K) helps regulate water balance and stomatal function, supporting water-use efficiency and helping crops maintain turgor during drought and heat stress.
- Magnesium (Mg) is essential for chlorophyll, photosynthesis and energy production, helping crops maintain photosynthetic activity during periods of stress.
- Zinc (Zn) supports antioxidant defence, root development and stress-response mechanisms, helping protect cells from the oxidative damage associated with drought and heat.
Understanding the plant’s nutritional requirements when water is in short supply and air temperatures are more than 35C can go a long way to helping them survive prolonged periods of stress, he explains.
“Timely use of these nutrients is something we are going to have to build more into future fertiliser plans,” says Tom.
Newly developed roots during seed germination contain up to 200ppm of zinc, which indicates the important role of this nutrient. For example, during early seed germination and seedling development.
“Mg and K are essential in the maintenance of photosynthetic carbon dioxide fixation and transportation of assimilates and key nutrients in chloroplasts with wheat plants enduring low Mg supply, in particular, being especially susceptible to heat stress.
“Wheat plants in drought situations with an adequate supply of K use approximately 12 times more carbon dioxide, a strong indication of the rate of photosynthesis taking place, than those with inadequate levels.”
Combining K with N in a balanced nutrition approach has been proven to significantly increase NUE and yields through a synergetic approach, he adds.
Results from the International Potash Institute show when N and K are applied separately, each element can produce a yield response of 2t/ha in wheat, but when combined this rises to 5t/ha.
“Potassium improves NUE by enabling better N uptake and utilisation with multiple experiments showing a typical K application of between 30-150kg K20/ha results in improved NUE of 10-40%.”
4. Embrace new technology and thinking
Fertiliser use is a major on-farm cost and one of the main contributors to the carbon footprint of production. Efficient use is essential.
“Routine soil testing is becoming widely adopted, but soil mapping and production of detailed nutrient plans are areas where new technology can really help boost input efficiency,” says Tom.
“Technology is moving quickly in crop nutrition – not just in terms of product development but with regard to support services to plan and monitor nutrient usage in cost-effective ways.”
Nutrition webinar
Agrii is hosting a 2026 post-harvest webinar on Tuesday 15th September at 08.30-10.00am looking at several aspects of crop nutrition and its management to maximise returns in 2027. The event is open to all farmers and growers and places can be reserved using the following link: https://www.agrii.co.uk/other-events/post-harvest-priorities-webinar-setting-crops-up-for-maximum-potential/

articles.title: ‘Why was mum in clothes you could wear in the winter?’: family seeks answers after care home heatstroke death - The Guardian
articles.search_term: (heatstroke OR "heat stroke" OR sunstroke OR "heat exhaustion" OR "heat-related death" OR "heat casualty" OR "heat fatality" OR "suspected heat death" OR dehydration OR "heat cramps" OR "heat illness") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
Anita Bazell had never coped with the heat very well, her family said. So they were worried about her when temperatures across the UK soared to record highs of 35C (95F) in May, and then again in June.
She was living in a nursing home in Southampton near her family, who had struggled to care for her at home due to her declining mobility. Although there were air conditioning units in the communal rooms, there was not one in Anita’s room, which was on the third floor.
“I used to see her every weekend. Heat rises and she was on the top floor, and the windows were open as far as the restrictors would let them go,” said her son, Steve Bazell. “It was hot in there. It was so hot you couldn’t sleep at night around here back then.”
The first phone call came on 25 June – Steve was told his mother was feeling unwell and she was being taken to bed. “I remember it because it was the hottest day on record [for June] that day,” Steve said. It was actually the second of three days that week when the temperature record for June was broken.
The next phone call, just after 9am the following day, was a shock. Paramedics called to say his mother had been found unresponsive and was being taken to Southampton general hospital. The family were urged to get there as soon as possible – medics were not sure she would make it to the hospital.
When they arrived, Anita’s face looked drooped on one side and they thought she had suffered a stroke. Doctors were putting towels soaked in ice water on her, replacing them every few minutes. The family were soon told she had been diagnosed with heatstroke, which had caused a bleed on the brain.
When she arrived in hospital, she had a body temperature of 41.2C – anything above 40C is considered a medical emergency.
“You could see her improving as she was getting cooler but she was still unresponsive,” he said. “We had mixed reactions. I mean, my mum was 88, but she was mentally fine. We couldn’t understand how this had happened – did they check on her?”
Anita was hospitalised on 26 June, which was then the hottest June day on record in the UK with 38C recorded at Lingwood in Norfolk, breaking the previous record of 35.6 degrees set in Southampton 50 years earlier. It was the fifth hottest day in the UK ever.
Steve was told Anita was one of at least seven elderly people taken to Southampton general hospital with heatstroke that day, and some did not make it there before they died.
The day before Anita’s admission, University hospital Southampton NHS foundation trust had declared a critical incident due to the extreme heat, which forced some operations and appointments to be cancelled.
David Higgs, the hospital’s deputy chief medical officer, later said Southampton general came “very close to collapse” during the June heatwave, which was “in many ways almost worse than Covid”.
“There was a huge amount of attendances in our emergency department. Primary care was overflooded. The ambulance service pretty much collapsed,” he told the city’s health and wellbeing board.
Steve said the hospital set up a special “cooling” ward specifically to deal with the influx of patients with heatstroke. Staff ran out of towels to soak in ice water to cool patients down, and resorted to cutting up bed sheets. “I remember I went upstairs to get more towels and help,” said Steve. “The hospital was really good. But they were stretched.”
Anita’s condition improved once her body temperature reduced, but ultimately there was nothing that could be done to save her. Over the next few days, Steve said her eyes would follow family members as they moved around her, and she could gently squeeze a hand when asked, but never regained full consciousness.
Steve and his sister took it in turns maintaining a bedside vigil every day until at least 10pm at night. He said they were a small but close family, and his mother devoted much of her life to supporting them.
As the siblings were growing up, Anita worked as a dinner lady and in their school library, volunteered as a Cub scout leader and supported them in their hobbies of motorbike racing and horse riding. She was married to her late husband, Les, for more than 50 years.
Anita died on 6 July with heatstroke recorded as her cause of death.
She is one of thousands of people believed to have died a heat-related death during the extreme hot weather this year. There were an estimated 2,877 heat-associated deaths in England during the May and June heatwaves, nearly double the 1,504 excess deaths recorded for the entire summer of 2025.
With four more heatwaves recorded across July and August, heat-related deaths this summer are expected to be the highest on record.
On 24 June, the Met Office issued a rare red heat weather warning due to the risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke, and predicted increased mortality and hospital admissions due to heat-related illness.
Some deaths may be linked to exertional heatstroke, caused by heavy physical exercise. Sophie Goodyer-Bird, a 35-year-old woman from Birmingham, died of heatstroke after climbing Yr Wyddfa – also known as Snowdon – on 10 July.
But most of the fatalities will be among the elderly population, although heatstroke is rarely recorded on death certificates as extreme heat often acts as an indirect trigger, placing severe strain on pre-existing health conditions that can be fatal.
Care homes for elderly people are on the frontline of dealing with this – during the July 2022 heatwave, nursing home deaths increased by 34.1% and residential care home deaths increased by 13.0%.
This year, many care homes reported using fans, air conditioners, paddling pools, ice lollies and cold fruit to keep residents cool. But research has found many are still underprepared for severe heat caused by the climate crisis.
The Care Quality Commission is investigating a care home in Watford after four residents were taken to hospital during the May heatwave, with one dying and the others “coming to harm”. An inspection report said there were concerns residents were left “at risk of dehydration”.
Anita’s family has written to her nursing home – which they have chosen not to name until investigations are complete – as they have concerns about the care she received in the hours before she collapsed.
After her death they were given the clothes she was wearing when she was brought into hospital, which Steve described as “a short-sleeve woolly jumper and wool trousers”. He said: “Why was mum in clothes you could wear in the winter? And how long had she been wearing them for?”
Steve said he wanted to raise awareness of the risks of heatstroke, particularly among elderly people in care homes, with more extreme heat on its way next year.
“They’re already saying it’s going to be hotter next year,” he said. “What my mum went through, what we went through as a family, it’s really not a very pleasant experience. I’m not saying it wouldn’t have happened anyway, but I do want to know if anything could have been done differently.”

articles.title: Feels like summer... Bengaluru sizzles at 32 degrees Celsius - The New Indian Express

articles.full_text:
BENGALURU: It is supposed to be summer with cloudy skies, rain and cooler weather in Bengaluru. But this September, it has been more like summer than the expected pleasant weather, because of clear skies and soaring temperatures. To top it off, the weatherman has sounded alerts for high ultraviolet (UV) radiation along with hot weather for most parts of Karnataka, including Bengaluru, over the next few days.
Bengaluru city has been recording a maximum temperature of 32 degrees Celsius over the last few days, while the average is around 28 degrees Celsius for September. As per India Meteorological Department (IMD) data, the city on Monday recorded a maximum temperature of 31.9 degrees Celsius, while on Sunday it was 32.2 degrees Celsius. The Kempegowda International Airport recorded 33.4 and 33.2 degrees Celsius, on Monday and Sunday, respectively.
N Puviarasan, director in-charge, IMD Bengaluru, said, “September temperatures have made the month feel like April, when summer is peaking. Poor monsoon has contributed to the rise in temperature.”
While a heat wave alert has been sounded for neighbouring states, including Andhra Pradesh, high temperatures have been forecast for Karnataka. On the UV alert, Puviarasan said hot weather has nothing to do with the radiation. As Bengaluru is at an elevation of 3,000ft and there is no cloud and water vapour, the radiation and moisture evaporation is high, making it hot in the state capital.
As per IMD data, most regions in the state, including Karwar, Honnavar, Dharwad, Gadag, Shivamogga, Chitradurga and Mandya, recorded the maximum temperature of 32 degrees Celsius on Monday. Mysuru recorded 34.2 degrees Celsius and Bagalkot 34.5 degrees Celsius.

MEMPHIS, Tenn. - HEAT ADVISORY FOR PARTS OF MID SOUTH FROM 11AM -8PM.
It's a comfortable start to the day with passing clouds.
Temperatures this afternoon will be in the upper 90s, near 100°. Feels like temperatures near 105°.
Rain chance: 10%.
Winds: 10 mph.
LOOKING AHEAD: Temperatures stay above average in the upper 90s tomorrow before dropping to low/mid 90s Wednesday through the end of the weekend. Rain chances return starting Thursday. Severe risk is low.
